title: Float the Bead
summary: Charge a metal bead so the push of a charged base floats it into a laser beam, then slide the laser to where a charged bead will float.
subject: physics
concepts: Solving Coulomb's law for the distance
learningOutcome: After winning, the student can balance the Coulomb push against weight, solve k q Q / h² = m g for the charge or the height, convert mg, mm, nC and pC to SI, and match the sign to the base.

levels.title: Float it
levels.adds: Baseline: set the bead's charge so the push from the base equals its weight exactly in the laser beam (Ex 1.1 and Example 1.3 at lab scale).
hints: The bead floats where the electric push equals its weight: k q Q / h² = m g.
Solve for q: q = m g h² / (k Q). Convert g, cm and µC to kg, m and C first.
Use g = 9.8 m/s² and k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Four times the charge floats the bead only twice as high.

levels.title: Tiny scale
levels.adds: Harder: milligrams, millimetres and nanocoulombs. Convert every prefix to SI, and the charge comes out in picocoulombs.
hints: 1 mg = 10⁻⁶ kg, 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, 1 nC = 10⁻⁹ C, 1 pC = 10⁻¹² C.
The balance is the same: q = m g h² / (k Q).
A result of 2.7 × 10⁻¹¹ C is 27 pC.

levels.title: Opposite base
levels.adds: New idea: the base may be negative. Only like charges repel, so choose the sign of the bead's charge as well as its size.
hints: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. To float, the bead must be pushed up.
Give the bead the same sign as the base. An opposite charge pulls it down onto the base.
Find the size exactly as before, with the sizes of the charges: q = m g h² / (k |Q|).

levels.title: Aim the laser
levels.adds: New idea: the bead's charge is given and you set the height. Solve Coulomb's law for the distance, h = √(k q Q / (m g)) (Ex 1.2a).
hints: The bead still floats where k q Q / h² = m g; this time h is the unknown.
Rearrange: h = √(k q Q / (m g)), with every quantity in SI units.
Convert the answer from metres to centimetres: 0.09 m is 9 cm.

misconceptions: Doubling the charge doubles the float height
Forgetting to convert prefixes (mg, mm, nC) to SI units
A bead with the opposite charge can still float
An uncharged bead is pushed up a little
